A test post exercising inline math, displayed equations, heavy sub/superscripts, and a short numbered proof.
KaTeX Rendering Test
This post exists to check that math renders correctly on nonelementary. Nothing here is deep — just enough logic to stress-test inline symbols, display equations, and dense subscript/superscript notation, including the cases (bare underscores, escaped braces, \\ line breaks) that markdown parsers tend to mangle.
Inline symbols
In first-order logic we write $\Gamma \vDash \varphi$ for semantic entailment and $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ for syntactic derivability. Soundness says $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ implies $\Gamma \vDash \varphi$; completeness gives the converse. Quantifiers $\forall x$ and $\exists x$ range over a domain, $a \in D$ is domain membership, $A \subseteq B$ is substructure inclusion, and set-builder notation like $\{x : \varphi(x)\}$ picks out a definable subset.
A displayed equation
The compactness theorem:
$$\Gamma \vDash \varphi \iff \text{there is a finite } \Gamma_0 \subseteq \Gamma \text{ such that } \Gamma_0 \vDash \varphi$$
And soundness/completeness together, as an aligned pair:
$$\begin{aligned} \Gamma \vdash \varphi &\implies \Gamma \vDash \varphi \quad \text{(soundness)} \\ \Gamma \vDash \varphi &\implies \Gamma \vdash \varphi \quad \text{(completeness)} \end{aligned}$$
Substitution, subscripts and superscripts
The substitution axiom schema of first-order logic:
$$\forall x\, \alpha \rightarrow \alpha^{x}_{t}$$
Here $\alpha^{x}_{t}$ denotes the formula obtained by replacing every free occurrence of $x$ in $\alpha$ with the term $t$, provided $t$ is substitutable for $x$ in $\alpha$ (no free variable of $t$ becomes bound). Substitutions can stack: $\big(\alpha^{x}_{t}\big)^{y}_{s} = \alpha^{x,y}_{t,s}$ when $x \neq y$ and neither substitution captures the other's variables.
A short numbered proof
Claim: $\vdash \alpha \rightarrow \alpha$, from the Hilbert-style axioms
$$A_1:\ \alpha \rightarrow (\beta \rightarrow \alpha), \qquad A_2:\ \big(\alpha \rightarrow (\beta \rightarrow \gamma)\big) \rightarrow \big((\alpha \rightarrow \beta) \rightarrow (\alpha \rightarrow \gamma)\big)$$
and modus ponens (MP).
$\alpha \rightarrow \big((\alpha \rightarrow \alpha) \rightarrow \alpha\big)$ — instance of $A_1$, with $\beta := \alpha \rightarrow \alpha$.
$\big(\alpha \rightarrow ((\alpha \rightarrow \alpha) \rightarrow \alpha)\big) \rightarrow \big((\alpha \rightarrow (\alpha \rightarrow \alpha)) \rightarrow (\alpha \rightarrow \alpha)\big)$ — instance of $A_2$, with $\beta := \alpha \rightarrow \alpha$, $\gamma := \alpha$.
$\big(\alpha \rightarrow (\alpha \rightarrow \alpha)\big) \rightarrow (\alpha \rightarrow \alpha)$ — MP on 1, 2.
$\alpha \rightarrow (\alpha \rightarrow \alpha)$ — instance of $A_1$, with $\beta := \alpha$.
$\alpha \rightarrow \alpha$ — MP on 4, 3.
$\blacksquare$

Why the blog is named after a theorem about finiteness, and what it's for.
Not first-order, not easy
In model theory, a class of structures is elementary if some single first-order theory axiomatises it exactly: $K$ is elementary iff there is a theory $T$ with $K = \{M : M \vDash T\}$. Most properties a working mathematician reaches for turn out not to be elementary, and finiteness is the standard example — the proof is short enough to write out in full.
Suppose $T$ is a first-order theory, in some language $\mathcal{L}$, with arbitrarily large finite models — a theory of groups, say, or of linear orders — and suppose, for contradiction, that every model of $T$ is finite. For each $n \geq 1$, let
$$\varphi_n \;\equiv\; \exists x_1 \cdots \exists x_n \bigwedge_{1 \le i < j \le n} x_i \neq x_j,$$
the sentence asserting at least $n$ distinct elements, and set $\Gamma = T \cup \{\varphi_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$. Any finite subset $\Gamma_0 \subseteq \Gamma$ mentions only finitely many of the $\varphi_n$, so some $N$ bounds the ones it contains; since $T$ has a finite model with at least $N$ elements, $\Gamma_0$ is satisfiable. By compactness, $\Gamma$ is satisfiable too — there is some $M \vDash \Gamma$. But $M \vDash \varphi_n$ for every $n$, so $M$ is infinite, while $M \vDash T$, contradicting the assumption that every model of $T$ is finite. No first-order theory can have exactly the finite structures as its models: finiteness is not elementary. Well-ordering fails to be elementary for the same reason, and so does torsion in groups.
Nonelementary is that theorem, and also a joke about how the subject feels twenty years after I last did any of it seriously.
I wrote an undergraduate thesis on Gödel's incompleteness theorems two decades ago. After that came a master's in logic and formal grammar, a PhD in computational linguistics, and a career in AI, over the course of which most of the logic itself quietly fell out of my head. This blog is where it's getting put back — evenings and weekends, alongside full-time work, which makes it a multi-year project rather than a course with an end date.
The field I work in now has no shortage of people who can build systems, and a real shortage of people who understand what is underneath them. I would like to be in the second group. I don't think there is a fast way to get there: it takes doing the proofs rather than reading about them, and it takes years rather than weekends.
What ends up here will mostly be notes from that work — proofs that took longer than they should have, places where the intuition was wrong, occasionally some history or philosophy when it changes how a piece of mathematics reads. There is no fixed schedule, and no promise that the whole plan survives contact with the material.
